description: Export eval (phase 6, extended in 11.1 and gate 11): tasks that need export, stats, texture maps, levels of detail, root motion and engine notes, and reading a .glb. Each names the files to save in the run folder; eval/export.ts checks them.

tasks.task: Export examples/ember-beetle.json as x01.glb with only two animations, its tripod cycle and its bite, at low mesh quality.
Generate an insect (any seed) and export it as x02.glb with the rpg game stats stored in the file.
Make a game-ready demon whose body is at most 1.2 m tall, with idle, walk, bite and roar animations, and export it as x03.glb.

A game needs three things about examples/ridgeback-stalker.json once exported: which node in the .glb a fire-breath effect should be attached to, how long the bite animation lasts in seconds, and at what time in the bite the jaw snaps shut (the moment to deal damage). Export it as x04.glb and write x04.json as { "node": …, "biteSeconds": …, "contactSeconds": … } with what you read from the file.
Export examples/grey-wolf.json as x05.glb with the sharpest texture maps the exporter offers, for a close-up cutscene.
A mobile game cannot afford texture maps. Export examples/cave-bat.json as x06.glb with its colours in the vertices only, and no images in the file.

Make a creature whose skin glows in the dark with a pulsing pattern, export it as x07.glb so the glow shows in a game engine, and write x07.json as { "pulseHz": … } with how many times a second its glow pulses, read from the exported file (the game animates the pulse itself).

Export examples/sand-cheetah.json as x08.glb. Its artist asks what will look different in the game engine than in the Spawnforge sandbox. Write x08.json as { "differences": [ … ] }, one short string per live effect the file leaves out or approximates, and { "furLengthMetres": … } in the same object with the fur length the file gives for the engine's own fur.

Export examples/tusk-boar.json as x09.glb. A game shows it on a 1080-pixel-high screen with a 60° vertical field of view. Write x09.json as { "skinTriangles": [full, level 1, level 2, level 3], "lowestFromMetres": … } with the skin's triangle count at each level, read from the file, and the distance in metres from which the coarsest level's error stays under one pixel.

A game needs a big cat that pounces. Give examples/sand-cheetah.json a pounce, export it as x10.glb and write x10.json as { "clip": …, "forwardMetres": … }: the name of the clip that moves the creature by itself, and how far forward (+Z) its root ends up at the clip's end, read from the file.

A Godot developer imports examples/grey-wolf.json as an export. Export it as x11.glb and write x11.json as { "loop": [ … ], "breathNode": … }: the names of the animation clips they should set to loop, and the name of the node a fire-breath effect should be parented to.
